feet.label: Leather-soled sandals tied with straps, suited to Roman roads.

head.label: A plain cloth wrapped over the head against sun and dust; hair kept short.

hold.label: A basket or pack for samples and small goods, since merchants carried wares and money on long trips.

figures.name: A Jewish merchant of the Diaspora

over.label: A wool mantle (himation, or Hebrew talit) with tassels at the corners, which Jewish men traditionally wore.

figures.signals: The practical tunic and travelling cloak suggest a trader who moved between cities. The tassels would mark him as a Jewish man who followed the Law.

under.label: A knee-length tunic of wool or linen, probably belted at the waist for travel.

figures.who: James 4:13-16 pictures traders who say they will go to a city, spend a year there and make a profit.

head.label: Bare head with neatly cut hair, in the Greco-Roman fashion.

hold.label: A scroll for accounts or contracts, since landowners kept written records of debts and sales.

figures.name: A wealthy landowner

over.label: A fine wool mantle dyed with costly purple dye, which only the wealthy could afford.

figures.signals: Fine linen and dyed wool showed wealth and status. Such clothing set the rich apart from the many who wore undyed wool.

under.label: A long linen tunic (chiton), a fine cloth that was costly in the eastern Mediterranean.

figures.who: The rich appear in the next passage (James 5:1-6), and James 4 warns against the pride and self-reliance seen in wealth and business plans.

head.label: A veil or head cloth covering the hair, as was customary for women in public.

hold.label: A clay water jar, carried daily for household water.

figures.name: A woman of a Jewish community

over.label: A wool shawl or wrap, here dyed blue with a common plant dye, draped over the shoulders.

figures.signals: Modest, plain clothing showed a respectable household of modest means. Dyed cloth was a sign of a little extra money.

under.label: A long wool tunic reaching the ankles, the usual dress of ordinary women.

figures.who: She stands for ordinary members of the scattered congregations that the letter addresses (James 1:1).

foods.name: Barley and wheat bread
foods.text: Flatbread baked at home was the daily staple, and the whole discussion of quarrels and desires in James 4:1-3 deals with the wish for goods and daily needs.

foods.name: Olives
foods.text: Eaten whole after curing in brine, they were a common food, and merchants traded them in the markets James describes.

foods.name: Olive oil
foods.text: Pressed from olives, it was used for cooking, lamps and trade, and was a major commodity in Mediterranean commerce.

foods.name: Diluted wine
foods.text: Wine was usually mixed with water at meals, and it was a staple of trade.

foods.name: Figs
foods.text: Eaten fresh or dried into cakes, they were a common food that stored well for travel.

foods.name: Water
foods.text: Drawn from wells and cisterns and carried in jars, it was a daily necessity, and James 4:14 compares life to a mist that soon vanishes.

objects.name: Letter scroll
objects.text: James is a letter, probably written on papyrus, and traditionally linked to James of Jerusalem; it was copied and passed among Jewish-Christian communities.

objects.name: Bronze and silver coins
objects.text: Traders used Roman and local coins to buy and sell, which is the setting for the plan to 'make a profit' in James 4:13.

objects.name: Merchant ship
objects.text: Sea trade linked cities of the Mediterranean, and a merchant might plan a year's trading trip by ship or road.

objects.name: Home meeting place
objects.text: Early congregations probably met in private homes, where the disputes in James 4:1-2 could arise.

objects.name: Clay water jar
objects.text: A common household vessel that held water, oil or grain, and an everyday item in homes like those James addresses.

objects.name: Travel sandals
objects.text: Leather sandals suited merchants walking Roman roads, as in the travel plans of James 4:13.

context.text: James is a letter, but it reads much like Jewish wisdom writing, with short commands, sharp contrasts, and vivid images. Chapter 4 quotes or echoes Proverbs 3:34 ("God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble"). The author also uses the prophets' language of unfaithfulness to God.
context.title: A letter in the style of wisdom teaching

context.text: The letter is in fairly refined Greek, which surprises some readers given its traditional author. Scholars debate whether James wrote it directly, had help from a skilled secretary, or whether it was composed later in his name. Greek was the common language of the eastern Mediterranean.
context.title: Written in polished Greek

context.text: The letter is addressed to "the twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1). This probably means Jewish Christians living outside Judea, though some scholars read it more widely. Its tone and its references to the law and to synagogue-style assembly fit that setting.
context.title: Jewish Christian audiences

context.text: Verses 13 to 17 picture people saying they will go to a city, spend a year, and make a profit. Trade by land and sea linked the cities of the Roman Empire. Small merchants took real risks, and plans could fail through illness, shipwreck, or death.
context.title: Traveling traders

context.text: Verses 1 to 3 speak of "fights and quarrels." Scholars debate whether this means literal violence, bitter verbal conflict, or rivalry within the congregations. Close-knit groups with little money and shaky status could easily have disputes over honor and resources.
context.title: Conflict inside communities

context.text: Verses 11 and 12 warn against speaking against or judging a fellow believer. The author treats the law as something to be kept, not sat in judgment over. In Jewish tradition, slander and false accusation were serious wrongs.
context.title: Judging a neighbor

context.text: The audience lived under Roman rule, with little political power. Honor, patronage, and wealth shaped who counted in society. The author's contrast between worldly ambition and humility plays against that background.
context.title: Life under Roman rule

firstHearers.text: The prophets often described Israel's disloyalty to God as adultery. Hearers familiar with Hosea or Ezekiel would recognize this as a charge of broken loyalty, not necessarily a charge about sexual behavior.

firstHearers.point: "Friendship with the world" was about loyalties
firstHearers.text: In the ancient world, friendship meant shared allegiance and obligation. To be a "friend" of the world meant adopting its values and alliances, which put one in opposition to God.

firstHearers.point: Honor and shame drove social life
firstHearers.text: Public status mattered enormously. Boasting, rivalry, and slander were ways of gaining honor, so the call to humility cut against ordinary expectations.

firstHearers.point: The letter was heard, not read privately
firstHearers.text: Most people encountered texts by hearing them read aloud in groups. Repeated commands and short, punchy lines suited listeners, and the rebuke was received in front of the whole community.

firstHearers.point: Plans were seen as under divine control
firstHearers.text: The phrase "if the Lord wills" (4:15) fits a widely shared Jewish view that human plans depend on God. Hearers would have heard a reminder of limits, in the tradition of Proverbs 27:1, not a ban on planning.

scene.heading: A Letter Read Aloud in a Gathering
scene.text: You sit on a bench or on the floor in a crowded room, probably in a believer's house. The air smells of lamp oil, wool, and dust from the street. A reader stands with a scroll or sheets of papyrus and reads in Greek. Around you are craftworkers, traders, and farmers in linen tunics and rough cloaks, with sandals worn thin. Some have come from the market, and their hands still carry the smell of fish, leather, or dyed cloth. Barley bread and olives wait on a low table for later. Outside, the flat-roofed houses of a Mediterranean town bake in the sun. Merchants plan journeys and talk of profits for the coming year. In the room, the reader's voice rises and falls. Words about quarrels, desire, pride, and the brevity of life carry across the room. A child shifts on a mat. Someone coughs. Everyone listens, since a letter like this is heard together, not read in silence.

date.label: Probably mid-1st century AD
date.note: The letter's date is debated: many scholars favour the AD 40s–60s, while others place it later in the 1st century or early 2nd.

setting.period: The Roman Empire rules the Mediterranean world, and Judea is under Roman authority, whether through client kings or governors, depending on the date.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.role: Tradition places James as leader of the church here, so it is the probable origin of the letter. James 4 itself does not mention it.

places.name: Antioch in Syria
places.role: A large trading city with an early Jewish Christian community. It is one possible kind of place where the letter's readers lived, but the text does not say.

places.name: Alexandria
places.role: A major port with a large Jewish population. It is an example of the Diaspora trading cities that fit the 'such and such a city' of 4:13, which names no real place.

places.name: Ephesus
places.role: A leading commercial centre of the Roman province of Asia. It illustrates the merchant world implied by the plans to travel, trade and profit in 4:13.

places.name: Rome
places.role: The imperial capital and the hub of Mediterranean trade. It is shown only as background to the travelling merchants of 4:13, and the letter does not name it.

setting.summary: James 4 is part of a letter to Jewish Christian communities outside the land of Israel. It criticises quarrels and rivalry, urges humility before God, warns against judging others, and challenges confident business plans made without thought for life's uncertainty.
setting.title: Warnings on Pride, Conflict, and Planning
setting.written: Traditionally written by James, a leader of the Jerusalem church and the brother of Jesus, who is said to have died around AD 62; some scholars think a later author used his name or his teaching.

words.here: James uses a prophetic image of broken covenant loyalty. The charge is about divided allegiance, not only about sexual conduct.
words.shift: In English this word names a sexual act and sounds harsh and old-fashioned. The Greek feminine form echoes the Old Testament picture of Israel as God's unfaithful wife. It is probably used figuratively for a whole community, not only women.
words.verse: You adulteresses, don't you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?

words.here: The word suggests choosing sides, not just liking something. It sets alliance with the world against alliance with God.
words.shift: Modern English friendship usually means casual warmth or companionship. In the ancient world philia could also mean a political or social alliance with shared loyalties. It is paired here with its opposite, hostility.
words.verse: don't you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?

words.here: The sense is a set of values and loyalties, not the created earth. That fits the quarrels and desires James describes.
words.shift: English world usually means the planet or all people. Kosmos originally meant order or decoration, and later the created order. Here it likely means human society organized apart from God, not the physical earth.
words.verse: friendship with the world is hostility toward God?

words.here: Translators differ on whether God's Spirit longs jealously for us, or whether human spirit tends toward envy. The quoted Scripture is also unidentified.
words.shift: Phthonos usually means envy of what others have, which is a vice. English jealously can sound like possessive love. The verse is hard to translate, and scholars disagree on its subject and tone.
words.verse: Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain, 'The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously'?

words.here: The picture is of a person with a split loyalty. It ties back to the earlier talk of serving both God and the world.
words.shift: English double-minded can sound like indecision or mixed opinions. Dipsychos is a compound meaning two souls. It is rare, and James is among the earliest writers known to use it.
words.verse: Cleanse your hands, you sinners; and purify your hearts, you double-minded.

words.here: James calls for deep, visible sorrow over wrongdoing. The tone is like that of the Old Testament prophets.
words.shift: The verse in the World English Bible reads 'Lament', which is how this word is rendered. Modern English lament suggests quiet sorrow or a song. The Greek is stronger and describes real misery and distress, and here it is a command.
words.verse: Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to gloom.

words.here: The issue is talk that lowers other people's standing. James then ties this to judging, which he says puts a person above the law.
words.shift: English speak against can mean any open disagreement. The Greek verb is built from words meaning down and talk, and it points to damaging someone's reputation. It is closer to slander or backbiting than to honest criticism.
words.verse: Don't speak against one another, brothers.

words.here: The image stresses how brief and uncertain life is. It backs up James's warning against confident business plans.
words.shift: English vapor sounds technical or scientific. The Greek word is an everyday image for steam or breath that quickly disappears. It may echo Old Testament wisdom imagery such as the Hebrew hevel, often translated breath or vapor.
words.verse: For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time and then vanishes away.
